newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Telecom NZ pledges to restore earnings growth.
newsitem.headline: Telecom NZ pledges to restore earnings growth.

text.p: New Zealand's largest listed company, Telecom Corp, on Tuesday pledged to revitalise flagging earnings growth and move aggressively into the new millennium with the rapidly evolving telecommunications industry.

Reporting an eight percent decline in third quarter net earnings to NZ$167.2 million (US$115 million), its first profit fall in four years, Telecom chief Executive Roderick Deane said cost reduction was a major issue for the company.
"That's going to be the name of the game for us, given the way competition is going," Deane said.

Telecom's profit for the nine months to December 31 was NZ$528.1 million, up 1.5 percent. While volumes growth remained strong, competition had seen prices fall, and operating expenses were up 10.7 percent in the nine-month period.
Brokers had downgraded earnings forecasts for Telecom prior to the result, which saw the share price fall over 60 NZ cents in three weeks.
Negative sentiment was compounded last week when Standard and Poor's downgraded Telecom to 'AA' from 'AA+'.
But the stock spiked 10 cents higher to NZ$6.96 on the profit report, with initial analysis suggesting the utlity's core earnings were still intact.
"There are a lot one-offs in there," said SBC Warburg head of equities Campbell Stewart. "There is still genuine growth there."
Telecom is actively moving to divest itself of loss-making Australian subsidiary Pacific Star, which depressed the third quarter result by $17 million and the nine-month profit by NZ$39.8 million.
And start-up costs associated with Telecom's Internet service provider Xtra and its First Media cable television services have also tugged on earnings.

"I think looking ahead to the future, as we get the Pac Star problems resolved and as we get Xtra and First Media into more strongly operational mode, the major challenge will be productivity improvements and cost control," Deane said.

"So long as we can get our costs down fast enough relative to the price declines and keep growing those business volumes, which we're determined to do, then we will see a resumption of earnings growth as the year progresses."
Deane said Telecom was planning a new series of cost reduction initiatives in 1997/98 and had asked shareholders Ameritech and Bell Atlantic to supply "some expertise".
While margins would continue to decline in the rapidly evolving and increasingly competitive telecommunications industry, Telecom was committed to continued earnings growth.

Deane said mobility and personalisation of telecommunications services was the big trend for the future, and Telecom was developing plans for the commercial launch of a new personal communications service (PCS), which it had been trialing since 1995.
PSC combined features from the cellular and fixed-line networks to allow the customer to carry their phone and personal number with them.
"We really see that the linkage between fixed-wire services and mobile services will be a big driver for our future as well as for the future of the industry," Deane said.
Telecom would also provide greater band width, partly though its planned cable rollout and partly though other technologies.
Telephone calls through the Internet were already being trialed, with a commercial service expected to be launched later this year, and shopping via the Internet was another "exciting development".
A further challenge for the company as the new millennium approached was adjusting its computer systems to accommodate the year 2000, Deane said, adding that costs of doing do would be "substantial".
